title: 23 low-regret recommendations for AI policy
gist: IFP's Tim Fist, Saif Khan and co-authors lay out 23 concrete 'low-regret' AI-policy recommendations spanning transparency, state capacity, risk management, verification, resilience, China competition, and diplomacy, designed to prepare the US for a possible future where automated AI R&D accelerates risk without slowing beneficial AI diffusion — including tighter chip export controls, an $84M+ CAISI, an AI Verification Consortium, biosecurity and cybersecurity resilience investment, and major grid and permitting reform to sustain the roughly 8-month-to-2-year US AI compute lead over China.

insights.claim: The authors argue that given substantial uncertainty about whether and how much automated AI R&D will accelerate AI capabilities and pose severe risks, the US should adopt 'low-regret' policies that impose low costs or deliver clear benefits even if those risks prove overblown, rather than doing nothing or imposing draconian restrictions.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Establishes the article's core investment-relevant framing: expect policy action calibrated to be cheap-if-wrong rather than either full deregulation or a blanket AI slowdown, shaping the realistic regulatory range for AI-exposed companies.
insights.locator: So to make policy preparation as targeted and low-regret as possible

insights.claim: The authors set five criteria for any 'pacing' intervention: target only activities that could cause serious and irreversible harm; minimize any slowdown in diffusion of existing AI capabilities and ideally accelerate it; impose low costs or deliver clear benefits even if the risks prove unlikely; avoid disadvantaging more cautious labs and countries; and avoid creating a new regulatory apparatus likely to be misused, e.g. by concentrating power in a small set of companies.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist investors and policy-watchers can use to evaluate whether any specific proposed AI regulation is likely to be well-targeted or overreaching.
insights.quote: Target only AI development activities that could lead to serious and irreversible harms.
insights.locator: we think any intervention should meet the following five criteria

insights.claim: The 23 recommendations span seven policy areas: transparency, state capacity, risk management, verification, AI resilience, competition with China, and diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Gives a structural map of where near-term US AI regulatory and spending activity is most likely to concentrate across seven distinct policy fronts.
insights.locator: We've identified 23 of them, and they span 7 areas

themes.theme: Transparency: opening the black box of automated AI R&D

insights.claim: AI capabilities in math and cybersecurity are doubling roughly every 7 and 5 months respectively, yet outside frontier AI companies it remains poorly understood how the underlying drivers of progress — better data, training algorithms, reinforcement learning, or scale — are unlocking these gains.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Establishes concrete, trackable doubling-time benchmarks (7 months for math, 5 months for cybersecurity) investors can use to monitor AI capability acceleration independent of any single lab's marketing claims.
insights.locator: AI now regularly makes impressive breakthroughs in math

insights.claim: The authors recommend frontier AI companies voluntarily return to historical norms of open scientific publication — citing that as recently as 2020 OpenAI published detailed GPT-3 architecture, training recipe, and data information, and in 2022 Google published detailed scaling laws — to rebuild industry transparency about the science of AI progress.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Notes a real historical shift from open to closed AI research practices at OpenAI and Google, relevant context for assessing how much competitive information frontier labs are now withholding from the market and public.
insights.quote: As recently as 2020, OpenAI published detailed information on the architecture, training recipe, and data of GPT-3, while in 2022, Google published detailed scaling laws
insights.locator: Disclosing information about the science of AI

insights.claim: The authors recommend Congress mandate transparency specifically around automated-AI-R&D risk management, incident reporting (the FRONTIER Act would require 72-hour reporting of critical safety incidents), whistleblower protections, and disclosure of company 'model behavior specifications' such as OpenAI's Model Spec and Anthropic's Constitution.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Flags specific pending legislation (FRONTIER Act, AI Incident Reporting Act, AI Whistleblower Protection Act) that would create binding disclosure and reporting obligations for frontier AI labs, worth tracking for compliance and disclosure risk.
insights.locator: Congress should legislate transparency about automated AI R&D risk management

themes.theme: Building US government state capacity on AI

insights.claim: The authors recommend Congress fund the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) with at least $84 million per year and roughly 184 staff, empowered to forward-deploy staff inside frontier AI companies, contract directly with labs on safety and security work, and report to a senior White House or cabinet-level official.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified ask ($84M/year, 184 staff, forward-deployed inside labs) that would materially expand direct government oversight presence at frontier AI companies if enacted — a concrete regulatory-exposure data point.
insights.quote: IFP previously recommended increasing CAISI staff to 184 personnel and giving it a budget of $84 million, and the America First Policy Institute recommended allocating $50–100 million to CAISI per year.
insights.locator: Congress should provide CAISI with the manpower

insights.claim: The authors recommend the Department of Commerce (where CAISI sits) become the US government's lead on frontier AI technology, coordinating with the NSA and CISA on cybersecurity risk, the CDC on biological risk, and Treasury on financial risk from AI R&D automation.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Signals which specific federal agencies (Commerce/CAISI as hub, plus NSA/CISA/CDC/Treasury) are likely to gain expanded AI-oversight roles and budget under this policy architecture.
insights.locator: CAISI should be the government's central hub

insights.claim: The authors recommend the NSA, CIA, and FBI establish an integrated, colocated mission organization focused on PRC technology targets — regulators, lab executives, IT systems, and semiconductor companies — combining HUMINT, SIGINT, and counterintelligence to track Chinese AI development and defend US AI companies from espionage.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Suggests a significant escalation of US intelligence-community focus on Chinese AI labs and on counterintelligence protection for US AI companies, relevant to assessing espionage and IP-theft risk facing frontier labs.
insights.locator: The NSA, Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) should therefore dedicate collection resources

insights.claim: The authors recommend CAISI develop public risk-management guidelines for rapid AI capability improvement, with input from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, SpaceXAI, SSI, Thinking Machines, and third-party evaluators like METR and Apollo, including 'if-then' commitments where crossing a capability or risk threshold triggers a specific mitigation or release decision.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Names the specific labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, SSI, Thinking Machines) expected to be brought into a formal government-coordinated risk-threshold framework, relevant for assessing coming compliance obligations across the frontier-lab peer set.
insights.locator: CAISI should develop guidelines for managing the risks of rapid AI capability improvement

themes.theme: Verification technology as the linchpin for any AI agreement

insights.claim: By some optimistic estimates, barely 50 people are working on AI verification technology worldwide, despite it being described as a likely precondition for any future US-China or industry agreement to manage AI R&D automation risk.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A striking scarcity data point (only ~50 people globally) identifying AI verification as a severely underinvested, potentially investable niche technical field given its stated strategic importance.
insights.quote: By some optimistic measures, barely 50 people are working on it worldwide.
insights.locator: However, no AI verification technology is yet mature

insights.claim: Absent further progress in AI verification technology — the ability for mutually distrustful parties like the US and China to confirm how AI compute is being used without revealing sensitive information — any future 'pacing' agreement on frontier AI development risks becoming a de facto pause rather than a targeted, verifiable limit.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Frames verification technology investment as a prerequisite for any negotiated US-China AI agreement to avoid defaulting to a blunt, economically costly full pause.
insights.quote: Absent further progress in AI verification technology, “pacing” frontier AI development could become a euphemism for pausing it.
insights.locator: If the nuclear arms control precedent is any indication

insights.claim: The authors recommend CAISI co-lead an AI Verification Consortium (AIVEC) with industry to fund hardware testbeds, philanthropically funded prize competitions, and construction of a pilot fully verifiable data center — citing the industry-funded ZPrize competitions, which distributed over $4 million for zero-knowledge cryptography and produced average speedups of 2.3x-11.3x (up to 150x in one category).
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A concrete public-private R&D funding vehicle (AIVEC) with a proven prize-competition precedent (ZPrize's 150x speedup) that investors in cryptography or AI-security startups should track for funding and partnership opportunities.
insights.quote: The industry-funded ZPrize competitions demonstrate a useful precedent: they distributed over $4M for speeding up zero-knowledge cryptography, producing average performance gains ranging 2.3x–11.3x and up to 150x in one category.
insights.locator: Lightweight prize competitions

insights.claim: The authors recommend DARPA and NSF run dedicated AI verification R&D programs, explicitly modeled on ARPA's Project Vela, the historical program that helped verify Soviet Union compliance with the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty for nuclear weapons testing.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Draws a direct historical analogy (Cold War nuclear-test verification) to frame the scale and national-security seriousness of the proposed federal AI-verification R&D investment.
insights.quote: This would follow the precedent of ARPA’s Project Vela, a project to verify Soviet Union compliance with the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty for nuclear weapons testing.
insights.locator: DARPA should run a verification program

themes.theme: Investing in AI resilience: cybersecurity and biosecurity

insights.claim: Historically, Chinese and open-weight AI models have lagged the US frontier by about 8 months, meaning a model with the capabilities of Anthropic's Claude Mythos will likely be widely deployable by Chinese organizations by the end of 2026 — giving the US only about 4 months to build resilience against the new risks this introduces.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A specific, dated timeline (Mythos-class capability reaching Chinese organizations by end of 2026, ~4-month US resilience-building window) directly relevant to near-term cybersecurity and biosecurity risk planning.
insights.quote: a model with the capabilities of Claude Mythos will likely be widely deployable by Chinese organizations by the end of 2026, giving the US around 4 months to build resilience against the new risks this introduces.
insights.locator: As recent incidents show, AI resilience is a worthwhile goal

insights.claim: AI cyber capabilities are doubling roughly every 5 months, and the authors recommend a national 'Operation Patchlight' program — a more ambitious version of Anthropic's Project Glasswing and OpenAI's Daybreak — that would use frontier AI to find and patch open-source code vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them, via a 3-year coordinated national effort.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Names specific existing lab programs (Anthropic's Project Glasswing, OpenAI's Daybreak) as templates for a proposed national vulnerability-patching initiative, relevant for cybersecurity vendors and critical-infrastructure defenders.
insights.quote: AI cyber capabilities are doubling roughly every 5 months, making cybersecurity an ongoing battle between offense and defense.
insights.locator: AI cyber capabilities are doubling roughly every 5 months

insights.claim: The authors propose 'The Great Refactor,' an initiative to use AI to automatically translate hundreds of millions of lines of insecure open-source code into memory-safe Rust, potentially set up as a Focused Research Organization to secure high-impact libraries by 2030 and save billions in cybersecurity costs.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A concrete, large-scale technical proposal (mass Rust migration) that could reshape demand for memory-safe language tooling and code-migration services if adopted as a funded national program.
insights.locator: "The Great Refactor": AI could automatically translate

insights.claim: The authors argue biosecurity is uniquely asymmetric because bioattacks are more bottlenecked by information and tacit knowledge — which AI directly erodes by removing friction to accessing it — while biodefense is more bottlenecked by physical properties like manufacturing capacity, meaning AI is poised to accelerate attackers' progress more than defenders'.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A structural argument for why bio-risk from AI is a priority area disproportionate to other risk categories, given the fundamental offense-defense asymmetry in how AI affects information versus physical bottlenecks.
insights.quote: attacks are relatively more bottlenecked by information and tacit knowledge, while defenses are relatively more bottlenecked by physical properties, such as manufacturing capacity and physical infrastructure.
insights.locator: Biosecurity is uniquely difficult

insights.claim: The authors recommend the CDC invest $80 million annually in a federal pathogen early-warning system that adds metagenomic sequencing to existing traveler, wastewater, and clinical surveillance networks to rapidly detect novel biological threats.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified biosecurity spending proposal ($80M/year) relevant to companies in genomic surveillance, wastewater testing, and pathogen-detection technology.
insights.quote: The CDC should invest $80M annually in a federal pathogen early-warning system, adding metagenomic sequencing to existing traveler, wastewater, and clinical surveillance networks
insights.locator: Detect threats before they spread widely

themes.theme: Extending the US AI compute lead over China

insights.claim: Due to compute export controls, US companies currently access approximately 10x more AI compute than Chinese companies, enabling US AI model capabilities to run roughly 8 months ahead of China's, though the authors argue this lead could be extended to over 2 years with tighter chip controls, action against adversarial distillation, and protection of model weights from theft.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: The single most quantified competitive-positioning stat in the piece (10x compute access, 8-month capability lead, potential 2-year lead) — a core benchmark for assessing US-China AI competitive dynamics and export-control policy risk.
insights.quote: US companies currently access approximately 10x more AI compute than Chinese companies
insights.locator: Due to compute export controls

insights.claim: Existing semiconductor manufacturing equipment (SME) export controls have already produced a 50-100x US production advantage over China in aggregate AI computing power, but this has translated into only a 10x compute-access advantage because the US has allowed China to access chips via legal sales like the NVIDIA H200, smuggling, offshore foundry production, and cloud access — with the White House asserting Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 model was trained on NVIDIA GB300s accessed via cloud services in Thailand.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A concrete, named example (Kimi K3 trained on NVIDIA GB300s via Thai cloud access) showing a specific export-control leakage channel, directly relevant to NVIDIA chip-export policy risk and enforcement gaps.
insights.quote: The White House has asserted the best current Chinese AI model — Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 — was trained on cutting-edge NVIDIA GB300s accessed via cloud services in Thailand.
insights.locator: The US compute production advantage of 50–100x

insights.claim: The authors recommend Congress pass the AI OVERWATCH Act to codify export restrictions on the most advanced US AI chips like the NVIDIA GB300, and the Chip Security Act to mandate privacy-preserving location verification of AI chips to prevent smuggling.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Names specific pending legislation (AI OVERWATCH Act, Chip Security Act) that would tighten NVIDIA GB300-class chip export rules and mandate hardware location tracking, directly relevant to semiconductor export-policy risk.
insights.locator: Congress should also pass the AI OVERWATCH Act

insights.claim: Countering 'adversarial distillation' — where Chinese AI companies train their models on the outputs of US frontier models to free-ride on expensive reinforcement-learning steps — could add approximately another 7 months to the US AI lead, per an industry estimate.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A quantified estimate (+7 months of lead) for the specific policy lever of countering distillation, useful for weighing the relative payoff of different China-competition policy tools.
insights.locator: If the US countered adversarial distillation

insights.claim: The Electric Power Research Institute projects data centers could consume 9 to 17 percent of US electricity by 2030, up from 4 to 5 percent in 2024, with a single AI model training run potentially requiring 4 to 14 GW by 2030, while new transmission projects still take about 10 years on average to permit and build.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A major, quantified power-demand forecast (9-17% of US electricity by 2030, up to 14 GW per training run) directly relevant to utility, grid-equipment, and power-generation investment theses tied to AI data-center buildout.
insights.quote: The Electric Power Research Institute now projects that data centers could consume 9 to 17 percent of US electricity by 2030, up from 4 to 5 percent in 2024
insights.locator: To maintain and increase America's AI compute lead

insights.claim: China generated more than twice as much electricity as the US last year (up from parity in 2010) and added more than 430 gigawatts of wind and solar capacity in 2025 alone, roughly the nameplate capacity of the entire US grid every few years.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A stark comparative power-buildout stat (430 GW added in one year) showing China's electricity-generation advantage is a structural constraint on the US's ability to out-build AI compute capacity, a key risk to the US-China AI lead thesis.
insights.quote: In 2025, China added more than 430 gigawatts of wind and solar capacity, and is on track to add similar amounts in coming years, essentially adding the nameplate capacity of the entire US grid every few years.
insights.locator: By contrast, China has a much larger power system

insights.claim: A supermajority of Americans, per a recent Gallup poll, oppose an AI data center being built in their area, with at least dozens of billion-dollar projects blocked or delayed in Q1 2026, 14 states considering statewide moratorium proposals, and New York and Texas both pausing or auditing new data center/grid approvals.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of mounting local political opposition to data center construction (14 states considering moratoria, dozens of projects blocked) — a material siting and permitting risk for anyone building or financing AI data center infrastructure.
insights.quote: A supermajority of Americans, in a recent Gallup poll, report opposing an AI data center in their area.
insights.locator: Continued AI leadership will require new data centers

insights.claim: The authors recommend Congress authorize a Grid Infrastructure Fund where participating data center developers pay for their own load costs and contribute to a ratepayer-protection insurance pool; a fund backed only by hyperscalers could mobilize an estimated $15 to 25 billion over five years.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified financing mechanism ($15-25B from hyperscalers alone) for grid buildout tied to data centers, relevant to utility and grid-equipment investment as well as hyperscaler capex planning.
insights.quote: A fund backed only by hyperscalers could mobilize an estimated $15 to 25 billion over five years, and federal lending authority and private co-investment could make it substantially larger.
insights.locator: Congress should also authorize a Grid Infrastructure Fund

themes.theme: Laying groundwork for US-China diplomacy on AI risk

insights.claim: Because training-compute efficiency may be improving 10x per year or more, the authors argue high-risk AI capabilities will eventually diffuse widely regardless of export controls, meaning it will eventually be in both the US's and China's interest to cooperate on managing AI R&D automation risks, drawing a parallel to how the US and Soviet Union cooperated on nuclear non-proliferation during the Cold War even while competing in other domains.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Frames eventual US-China AI cooperation as a likely long-term outcome despite current competitive dynamics, an important scenario for geopolitical-risk modeling of AI policy beyond the near-term compute race.
insights.quote: the US and the Soviet Union managed to cooperate on nuclear non-proliferation during the Cold War
insights.locator: It is therefore valuable to lay the foundation

insights.claim: The authors recommend the US use its bilateral AI dialogue with China — referencing the Trump Administration's planned September 2026 AI risk dialogue — to jointly develop risk-management guidelines and prepare verification measures, building on the Frontier AI Safety Commitments both US and Chinese AI companies signed at the 2024 AI Seoul Summit.
insights.speaker: Tim Fist
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, dated near-term diplomatic event (September 2026 US-China AI risk dialogue) as a concrete milestone to watch for early signs of AI-related US-China cooperation or friction.
insights.locator: The Trump Administration's September 2026 AI risk dialogue
